title: syscall-batching-context-switch-costs-investigation
content:
Summary

This note captures an investigation into CPU-side latency contributions from frequent syscalls and context switches in the serving stack. It was prompted by recurring small-request tail spikes (~95th-99th percentile) where per-request CPU time is dominated by kernel transitions and short-lived thread handoffs rather than model compute. The goal was to measure the cost of different syscall patterns, validate whether batching reduces per-request overhead, and identify practical mitigations we can roll into the runtime.

Background and motivation

Symptoms observed:
- Spiky P95/P99 latencies on small payloads (<= 200 tokens) where model kernels are cheap (tied to small batches and short generation).
- Flamegraphs for these requests show many thin stacks in user space interleaved with frequent "syscall" markers, and worker threads scheduling in/out rapidly.
- Correlation between spikes and traffic with many short-lived requests (~2–10 ms per request in pure user CPU when aggregated).

Hypothesis:
1) Per-request syscall frequency (reads, writev, epoll_wait, accept, timerfd) and the resulting context switches are non-negligible and dominate CPU time when model time is small.
2) Syscall batching (coalescing writes, using pread/pwrite alternatives, using io_uring or splice/sendfile where applicable) and reducing thread handoffs can measurably reduce tail latency and CPU cost for small requests.

Experiment overview

What we measured:
- Microbenchmarks for common request I/O patterns: small read/write, writev with multiple iovecs, epoll_wait wakeup cost with a single wakeup, timerfd wakeups, and accept+handshake path.
- End-to-end synthetic request replay against a lightweight model stub that simulates model compute (0.5–3 ms) to measure overall per-request CPU and wall latency with different I/O strategies.
- Sampling profilers and perf stat counters for context switches (voluntary/involuntary) and syscalls per second.

Testbed and methodology:
- Instance: c6i-like 16 vCPU equivalent, Linux 6.x kernel with liburing available. Containers pinned to CPU cores with CPU isolation (no other noisy processes).
- Runtime under test: modified request dispatcher that supports three I/O modes: baseline (blocking read/write + epoll), batched writes (accumulate response iovecs into a single writev), and io_uring-based submission with SQE batching.
- Synthetic workload: POOL of 1024 concurrent lightweight clients issuing 1–3 requests each at controlled inter-arrival rates to force many small concurrent requests. Request payloads small (100–400 bytes). Model stub sleeps for configurable user-space compute to simulate model time.
- Observables: per-request wall latency (P50/P90/P95/P99), user CPU time, syscalls per request, voluntary context switches per request, scheduler latency (from ftrace markers), and throughput.

Key microbenchmarks and results (high level)

1) Single write vs batched writev
- Baseline: runtime writes response headers and body in 3 separate write() syscalls on average.
- Batched writev: coalesced into 1 writev syscall.
- Result: Per-request wall latency reduced by ~8–12% at P95 and ~15–22% at P99 for the smallest simulated model time (0.5 ms). Syscalls/request dropped from ~4.2 to ~1.3 (including epoll/accept). CPU user time per request decreased by ~6%.

2) epoll wakeup and handoff cost
- Observed that wakeups for worker threads (epoll_wait -> user code -> immediate epoll_wait) create a lot of voluntary context switches.
- Using the epoll EPOLLONESHOT + application-managed rearm to avoid redundant wakeups reduced voluntary context switches by ~35% and improved tail latency by ~10%.

3) io_uring submission queue batching
- Replacing immediate syscalls with io_uring submissions batched (submit multiple SQEs before entering kernel) reduced syscall transitions measured by perf by ~60% for the I/O path and improved P99 wall latency by ~18% for small requests.
- Note: benefits are largest when model stub compute is sub-ms to a few ms; for longer model kernels (>= 10 ms) overhead is amortized and gains are smaller.

4) context-switch analysis and scheduler wake queues
- Flamegraphs and perf sched trace revealed many sub-millisecond user-space slices preempted to perform small syscalls or timerfd callbacks. These slices add up when there are many requests per second.
- Reducing timerfd granularity and grouping timers reduced preemption churn; however, overly coarse timers introduced latency variance. Tradeoff window identified: group timers up to 2 ms without materially worsening P50.

Artifacts and measurements (representative)

- Example counters (small-request workload; simulated model compute = 0.5 ms):
  - baseline: syscalls/request = 4.2, voluntary context switches/request = 5.6, P99 latency = 28.3 ms
  - writev batching: syscalls/request = 1.3, voluntary CS/request = 4.2, P99 latency = 23.5 ms
  - io_uring batching: syscalls/request = 1.0, voluntary CS/request = 3.8, P99 latency = 18.4 ms

- Profiling notes: flamegraphs show long flat regions labeled as "syscall" and many shallow user frames. Sampling shows stack-aggregations around epoll_wait -> accept -> worker-handoff logic.

Interpretation and discussion

- When model compute time is small, kernel transitions and scheduler overhead are a dominant fraction of tail latency. Each syscall and context switch contributes tens to hundreds of microseconds depending on the scenario and kernel configuration.
- Batching I/O at the runtime boundary has a consistent, measurable effect on both tail latency and CPU efficiency. The simplest win is reducing multiple fragmented writes into a single writev or sendmmsg where applicable.
- io_uring provides the biggest wins in our testbed, but it comes with portability and implementation complexity tradeoffs (interoperability with existing epoll-based codepaths, need for thread model changes for submission completion handling, subtle interaction with memory registration and zero-copy).
- Some benefits can also be realized by reducing wakeups and reentrant worker handoffs (EPOLLONESHOT, careful rearming, sticky worker assignment for short-lived requests).

Risks and constraints

- Kernel behavior differs across distributions and versions. io_uring improvements measured on Linux 6.x may be muted on older kernels; we need kernel compatibility testing.
- Coalescing timers and batching can increase median latency for some traffic shapes; must be configurable and adaptive.
- Changing threading/wakeup semantics risks regressions under high load (convoys) and requires careful testing with chaos/integration suites.

Actionable recommendations

Short-term (safe, low-risk)
- Implement write coalescing in the dispatcher for HTTP and binary protocols: accumulate response headers+body/frames into a single iovec and use writev.
- Introduce EPOLLONESHOT rearm pattern for worker handoff paths to reduce unnecessary wakeups. Add toggles and metrics to track wakeups per request.
- Adjust default timer grouping to 1–2 ms with runtime-configurable knob.

Medium-term (moderate complexity)
- Prototype an io_uring submission path behind a feature flag with fallbacks to epoll. Start with request response write path and submission queue batching only (keep completion handling in user thread to avoid complexity).
- Instrument and baseline on kernels we support (Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, RHEL 9.x) to quantify portability impact.

Long-term (higher effort, higher payoff)
- Consider a hybrid submission model: use io_uring for I/O-heavy micro-requests while keeping heavier model compute on the existing path; orchestrate routing decisions by request size and model expected compute time.
- Explore lightweight user-level scheduling to reduce kernel handoffs for short-lived request processing, e.g., cooperative scheduling for request handlers to minimize preemption.

Next steps and experiment plan

1) Roll writev coalescing into canary branch, run 2-week A/B on staging and traffic replay to validate: metrics to watch — P95/P99 latency, syscalls/sec, voluntary context switches/sec, CPU utilization.
2) Enable EPOLLONESHOT rearm in canary and measure wakeup reductions and any convoys under synthetic high load.
3) Upstream a small io_uring prototype PR for the write path: keep it behind a feature flag and add runtime kernel-version gating.
4) Add detailed perf and ftrace captures for production spike diagnostics: add an automated capture recipe to ops runbook when P99 > baseline + X.

Open questions

- For production multi-tenant hosts, does io_uring submit batching interact poorly with noisy neighbors (e.g., starvation of completion handling)?
- What is the cost of memory pressure from larger batched iovecs on the allocator and caching behavior?
- Can we identify request-level heuristics to route micro-requests to specialized worker pools with different I/O strategies to reduce risk?

Appendix: quick reproduction steps

1) Clone the benchmark harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks (branch: syscall-batching-experiments).
2) Build the stub server (Makefile target: bench-stub).
3) Run server pinned to cores 4–11: TASKSET=0xFF ./bench-stub --mode=epoll --timer-group-ms=1
4) Run client replay script with small_payload.yaml workload (scripts/replay_small.sh).
5) Collect perf counters: sudo perf stat -e syscalls:sys_enter_write,syscalls:sys_enter_read,context-switches -p <pid> -- sleep 30
6) Capture flamegraph via simpleperf or 1-second sampling spectrogram script in tools/

Notes

- Full raw logs, perf stat dumps, and a few sample flamegraphs are attached in the linked Confluence page.
- This doc focuses on CPU/syscall angle; follow-on work should correlate with model kernel traces and GPU overlap to make routing decisions that consider compute vs I/O trade-offs."
